newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil port strike unwelcome disruption for coffee.
newsitem.headline: Brazil port strike unwelcome disruption for coffee.

text.p: Brazilian coffee exports should not be greatly affected by a strike by stevedores at the key port of Santos which is set to spread to a national level on April 4 but the stoppage is unwelcome, exporter officials said.

"Any change that you have in shipping schedules is unwelcome when international roasters are operating on a hand-to-mouth basis," said Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation.
"With the low stocks in consumer hands we have at the moment, any strike is very sensitive for the market," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Association.

Stevedores at Santos began a two-day strike today at 0700 local/1000 GMT over a court ruling which allows workers from steel mill Companhia Siderurgica Paulista (Cosipa) to conduct loading and unloading operations at Cosipa's terminal.
Union officials say by federal law only registered and qualified workers are allowed to do these jobs.

Concern other ports will see similar rulings has prompted the national stevedores federation to call a nationwide 24-hour strike on April 4 and federation officials have not ruled out the possibility of further stoppages.
Santos is Brazil's largest coffee exporting port, accounting for 984,698 60-kg bags of the 1.28 million loaded for March by March 31, according to today's Rio de Janeiro Coffee Bulletin.
A further 238,647 bags has been loaded at Vitoria, 51,865 bags at Rio de Janeiro and 1,245 bags at Varginha.
Overall, March shipments are expected to finish at between 1.35 million to 1.4 million bags.
April shipments, which are those directly affected by the stoppage, are also expected to be possibly around the same level with registrations for April at 1.40 million bags by March 21.

Dissatisfaction on the part of individual unions with other aspects of the government's port privatisation program could lead some other ports to begin striking April 3, said the president of Vitoria's stevedores union.
Under the program, manpower services have been privatised with the introduction of labor management bodies, known as OGMOs, which include representatives of shipping companies and labor unions.
"We are unhappy with the OGMO on issues such as payment and so we are deciding today whether to strike as of April 3," said Vitoria's Jose Adilson Perreira.
Other unions are discussing whether to join the stevedores in the national stoppage on April 4.
But as seen in Santos today, a strike just by stevedores effectively brings loading and unloading operations of key commodities such as coffee to a halt, officials said.
